doc.title: Lou Marini interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 15, 2023

title: Improvising over one chord versus changes
summary: Negotiating a vamp versus 'Body and Soul', learning by ear, theory following creativity, and Cannonball on 'Autumn Leaves'.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Let me go back a bit — you said improvising is a mysterious art — a mysterious thing to do. When you play a solo, an improvised solo over a one or two chord vamp or a 12-bar blues, is what’s going on in your head different than what you would play on “Giant Steps”? Or even “Body and Soul.” In other words more chord changes — how do you negotiate the challenging chord changes of a song as opposed to a one chord vamp?

Each of them presents their own challenges. The thing about playing over one chord is to not resort to hot licks, you know, modal patterns and stuff that you practiced. And I think so much of it just depends on the players you’re playing with. If you’re playing with creative players then somehow you’re being presented with alternate pathways or suggestions or prompts or opportunities to go different places you know. And, or you could play something that they respond to and that leads you to another place. Playing a tune like “Body and Soul” to me, which is a tune I like to play you know, the challenge there is to find, you know like Eddie Daniels talked about, playing a sequence, a melodic sequence that goes through a set of chord changes so that the sequence isn’t just root- minor third-fourth-sixth — now when you get to the major chord it’s got to be root-major third-fifth. That, finding those pathways — but you know I don’t think that the guys that we loved, I don’t think they thought about chord changes in the same way. I think their ear — I mean I learned to play by ear and by playing along with records. So I didn’t know what the hell I was doing as far as what chord changes and what the chord scale was. The theory, my dad used to always say that the theory comes after the guys who push us, and not just guys of course, women too who push us to another realization of harmony or whatever. Like Ravel had his shit together and then we’re all still playing the chord changes that we like, like Ivan Lins you know. That’s another thing that like I think about, man when you — like bossa nova harmonies, which everybody plotzes over, you listen to contemporary radio, you never hear a set of chord changes like that. You’re only hearing triads now you know.

I liked what you said about the theory coming after the creativity. Every once in a while I put on Cannonball’s, one of his very first records with Miles was on it, and they played “Autumn Leaves.” And the solo that Cannonball plays is utterly fascinating. And he’s got all these sort of not-in-the-chord tones, but the way he fashions them I’m just in awe.
